paragraphs.heading: The weight of the air
paragraphs.text: Atmospheric pressure, also called air pressure or barometric pressure, is the pressure within Earth's atmosphere. Pressure means force spread over an area, and its SI unit is the pascal, which is one newton per square metre. In most cases, air pressure nearly equals the pressure made by the weight of all the air above the point where you measure. That weight comes from the planet's gravity pulling on the gases above the surface.

paragraphs.heading: A column of air
paragraphs.text: Picture a column of air one square centimetre across, reaching from sea level to the top of the atmosphere. On average it has a mass of about 1.03 kg and presses down with about 10.1 newtons, which works out to roughly 101 kilopascals. In imperial units, a column one square inch across weighs about 14.7 lbf, giving 14.7 lbf/in². The link is P = F/A = (m*g)/A, so pressure follows the weight of air resting on each unit of area.

paragraphs.heading: Units and sea level
paragraphs.text: The standard atmosphere, written atm, is a unit defined as 101.325 kPa, the same as 1,013.25 hPa, 760 torr or about 14.696 psi. It roughly matches the average pressure at sea level on Earth. Weather reports normally give mean sea-level pressure, where readings from places above or below sea level are adjusted to sea level. That average is 1,013.25 hPa. Surface pressure, the pressure actually found on land and ocean surfaces, averages 985 hPa.

paragraphs.heading: Thinner air up high
paragraphs.text: Climb higher and less air sits above you, so pressure falls. That is why air pressure on mountains is usually lower than at sea level. Because the atmosphere is thin compared with Earth's radius, gravity can be treated as constant through it and adds little to this drop. Temperature and humidity also affect pressure, and both are needed to work out an accurate figure.

paragraphs.heading: Highs and lows
paragraphs.text: Air pressure varies widely across Earth, and those differences matter for studying weather and climate. The highest sea-level pressures occur in Siberia, where the Siberian High often tops 1,050 hPa and records come close to 1,085 hPa. The highest sea-level-adjusted reading taken above 750 m was 1,084.8 hPa, at Tosontsengel, Mongolia, on 19 December 2001. At the other extreme, the centres of tropical cyclones and tornadoes hold the lowest, with a record of 870 hPa.

paragraphs.heading: Tides in the air
paragraphs.text: Some pressure changes are very regular, and atmospheric tides are an important source of them. These tides are strongest in the tropics, where they swing by a few hectopascals, and nearly vanish in polar areas. In the tropics they are mainly two cycles laid on top of each other, one lasting 24 hours and one lasting 12.
